l1: Knowing a territory well enough to predict what it will offer, and when.
l2: A landscape held in the head is a map of water, stone sources, seasonal fruiting, animal routes and safe crossings. It is the difference between wandering and moving with intent, and it is knowledge that only pays off over years — which means it has to be transmitted, not learned fresh.
l3: Raw-material sourcing is the hard evidence. Geochemical fingerprinting matches stone artefacts to specific outcrops, letting archaeologists map the territory a group actually used. Some assemblages contain material from several hundred kilometres away.
ev: Geochemical sourcing of lithic raw material

l1: Following the year around a territory rather than staying put.
l2: Resources are not evenly distributed in time. A group that moves on a schedule tuned to fruiting, spawning and migration harvests the peak of each rather than the average of one place. It is a strategy that requires knowing the calendar of a landscape before the calendar exists.
l3: Seasonality is read from remains that grew in a known season: fish otoliths and shellfish shells lay down growth rings, and tooth cementum in mammals bands annually. These indicate the season of death, so a site can be shown to have been occupied only in autumn, or only in spring.
ev: Growth-increment seasonality; site occupation patterns

l1: Several people acting on one intention that none of them holds alone.
l2: Human cooperation is unusual in scale and in who it includes. Most animals cooperate with kin; humans cooperate routinely with strangers, sustained by reputation, reciprocity and shared norms rather than relatedness. Every institution later in this graph is an attempt to make that work at larger scale.
l3: Cooperation is visible archaeologically as tasks no individual could complete: large-game drives, structures needing many hands, and the movement of material through exchange networks between groups.
ev: Communal hunting sites; exchange networks; large structures

l1: Moving into land where nobody you know has ever lived.
l2: Humans occupied nearly every terrestrial environment on the planet without evolving specialised bodies for any of them. That is a technological and cultural achievement rather than a biological one — clothing, fire, shelter and transmitted local knowledge did the work that fur and fat do for other species.
l3: Genetics and archaeology are now read together. Ancient DNA from human remains reconstructs population movement and mixture directly, and it has repeatedly overturned tidy migration stories built on artefact styles alone.
ev: Ancient DNA; dated site sequences; artefact distributions
caution: Migration routes and dates are revised frequently as ancient DNA accumulates. Treat any specific route as provisional.

l1: Solving a climate with equipment instead of with a body.
l2: Adapting culturally is far faster than adapting genetically — a new garment design spreads in a generation, a new metabolism takes thousands. This is the central reason a single species with almost no anatomical variation occupies the Arctic, the Sahara and the high Andes at once.
l3: Cold-climate occupation leaves a distinctive toolkit: eyed needles, insulated dwellings, fuel management, fat-rendering equipment. Sites at high latitude and altitude are dated to show when each threshold was crossed.
ev: Cold-climate toolkits; high-latitude site dating

l1: Getting to the other side of water you cannot wade or swim.
l2: Water is the hardest barrier on a map, and crossing it opens land nobody else has claimed. Reaching Australia required open-sea voyages of tens of kilometres, across water that was never dry even at lowest sea level — which makes it the earliest strong evidence for watercraft anywhere.
l3: The reasoning here is geographic rather than artefactual: no boat survives, but sea-level reconstruction shows the gaps that had to be crossed, and dated occupation on the far side shows they were. Absence of the vessel does not weaken the inference.
ev: Palaeo-sea-level reconstruction; dated island occupation

l1: Buoyant material tied together until it carries weight.
l2: A raft floats by displacement and needs no hull, no shaping and no watertight joint — which makes it the lowest-technology way to move mass across water. It is slow and hard to steer, and it still changes what is reachable, especially along rivers and coasts.
l3: Direct evidence is essentially nil; organic craft do not survive. Experimental voyages using period-plausible materials test whether particular crossings were feasible, which constrains the possibilities without proving any one case.
ev: Experimental voyaging; inference from island colonisation
caution: No prehistoric raft survives. Reconstructions are plausibility tests, not artefacts.

l1: A shaped hull that displaces water and keeps its cargo dry.
l2: A hull can be steered, loaded and driven against a current in ways a raft cannot. Boats make rivers into roads. For most of history, moving goods by water was an order of magnitude cheaper than moving them by land, which is why almost every early city sits on a waterway.
l3: The Pesse canoe from the Netherlands, a hollowed pine log roughly 10,000 years old, is among the oldest surviving boats. Waterlogged burial preserved it. Earlier watercraft are inferred from island settlement rather than recovered.
ev: Waterlogged dugout finds; island colonisation dates

l1: Knowing where you are and which way to go with no landmarks in sight.
l2: Open water removes every reference a land animal uses. Navigators replaced them with star paths, swell direction, cloud behaviour over unseen islands and bird flight — a system held entirely in memory and taught by apprenticeship. Pacific voyagers crossed thousands of kilometres of ocean this way.
l3: Pacific navigation traditions were documented ethnographically while still practised, and have been tested by instrument-free voyages on reconstructed craft. Settlement chronologies across Oceania independently confirm the routes.
ev: Documented navigational traditions; instrument-free voyages

l1: Nets, weirs, traps and hooks — catching more than you could by hand.
l2: A net turns fishing from an individual pursuit into a harvest, and a fixed weir turns it into infrastructure that works while you sleep. This is the point where an aquatic food source becomes reliable enough to build a settled life around, sometimes long before farming.
l3: Fish weirs survive as stake alignments in waterlogged ground and can be radiocarbon dated. Net sinkers, shell hooks and mass fish-bone deposits in middens show scale of catch rather than mere presence.
ev: Dated fish weirs; net weights; midden fish assemblages

l1: A dwelling built to outlast the season.
l2: Building for permanence changes the economics of effort. A structure you will return to is worth a stone footing, a dug floor and a proper hearth — investments that make no sense in a shelter you abandon in a week. Permanence also makes possessions worth having, since they no longer have to be carried.
l3: Substantial construction shows as dug floors, stone foundations, heavy post-holes, repeated re-flooring and thick occupation deposits. Depth of accumulation distinguishes long residence from repeated brief visits.
ev: Dug floors; stone footings; deep occupation deposits

l1: Staying in one place long enough that the place becomes yours.
l2: Sedentism preceded farming in several regions rather than following it — where wild resources were rich and predictable enough, people settled first and cultivated later. Once settled, birth spacing shortens, possessions accumulate, refuse becomes a problem and land becomes something to hold.
l3: Sedentism is inferred from a bundle: heavy immovable equipment such as grinding slabs, year-round seasonality indicators, commensal animals like house mice and sparrows, and deep midden accumulation.
ev: Immovable equipment; year-round seasonality; commensal species
caution: Settlement did not always follow agriculture. In several regions the sequence runs the other way.

l1: More people, packed more densely, than mobile life allows.
l2: Settled life shortens the interval between births, because a mother no longer has to carry each child across a landscape. Denser populations mean more minds and more hands — and also crowd diseases, more conflict over land, and a much harder floor to fall back to if the harvest fails.
l3: Population is estimated from settlement area and house counts, and cross-checked against skeletal indicators of health and stress. The skeletal record often shows declining stature and increased disease markers with early farming, alongside rising numbers.
ev: Settlement-size estimates; palaeodemography; skeletal stress markers
caution: More people is not the same as better off. Early farming populations frequently show worse individual health than the foragers they replaced.

l1: Different people doing different work, and trading the results.
l2: Specialisation raises skill because practice concentrates, and it raises output because switching costs disappear. It also creates dependency: a full-time potter does not grow food and will starve without someone who does. Every complex society is a machine for managing that mutual dependency.
l3: Craft specialisation shows as standardised output — vessels of consistent form and fabric, produced in quantity, in workshop areas with production debris. Skeletal markers of repetitive occupational stress point the same way.
ev: Standardised craft output; workshop debris; occupational skeletal markers

l1: Deciding who gets what, and keeping some back for later.
l2: A stored surplus has to be governed. Who may draw on it, how much is held for seed, what happens in a bad year — these are questions with no natural answer, and the ways societies answered them became the first institutions. Management of stock is where politics starts.
l3: Communal storage facilities, standardised measuring vessels and — later — accounting tokens indicate deliberate allocation. Placement of granaries, whether in individual houses or in a shared central structure, distinguishes household from communal control.
ev: Communal granaries; standard measures; accounting tokens

l1: Knowing which plants feed you, which cure you, and which kill you.
l2: Foraging societies routinely command detailed knowledge of hundreds of species — where each grows, when it ripens, how it must be processed, what it treats. This body of knowledge is the entire precondition for agriculture. Nobody domesticates a plant they do not already understand.
l3: Starch and phytolith residues on tools, plant remains in hearths and dental calculus, and coprolite analysis together reconstruct the plant component of ancient diets — a component the bone-heavy record systematically undercounts.
ev: Phytoliths; starch residues; dental calculus; coprolites

l1: Keeping the best seed to plant rather than eating it.
l2: This is a genuinely difficult decision: setting aside good food now for a benefit that arrives months later and may not arrive at all. Repeated over generations, it also does something nobody intended — it changes the plant, selecting for larger grain and for seed heads that stay attached instead of shattering.
l3: Domestication is visible in the seeds themselves. Grain size increases and the rachis — the attachment point — becomes tough rather than brittle. Both changes are measurable in charred assemblages, and they appear gradually over centuries.
ev: Grain-size series; rachis morphology in charred assemblages

l1: Deliberately making a place better for the plants you want.
l2: Cultivation starts long before domestication: clearing competitors, watering, burning to encourage regrowth, sowing gathered seed. It is a spectrum of intervention, not a switch, which is why 'the invention of agriculture' is a misleading phrase for a process that took thousands of years.
l3: Weed floras give it away. Cultivated ground supports a distinctive community of disturbance-loving species, and their appearance in archaeobotanical assemblages signals tillage before the crops themselves show domestication traits.
ev: Arable weed assemblages; field systems; tillage marks

date: ≈ 11,000 years ago onward, independently in several regions
l1: A species reshaped by living alongside humans, over generations.
l2: Domestication is mutual. Humans changed wheat, cattle, rice, maize and dogs; those species changed human diet, settlement, labour and disease exposure in return. It happened independently in at least eleven regions with different species — which makes it a repeated response to conditions, not a single invention that spread.
l3: Morphological change is visible in bones and seeds; genomic change is now readable directly from ancient DNA, which can date and locate domestication events and detect the repeated mixing between wild and domestic populations.
ev: Morphological change; ancient genomes; regional chronologies
caution: Domestication arose independently in multiple regions. There is no single origin point, and no evidence of a plan.

l1: Managing animals on the hoof instead of hunting them.
l2: A herd is a food store that walks. It converts grass — which humans cannot eat — into milk, meat, hide, wool and traction, and it can be moved to land too dry or steep to farm. Herding also brings people into close, permanent contact with animals, with consequences for disease that nobody anticipated.
l3: Kill-off patterns are the key: hunted populations show a natural age spread, managed ones show culling of young males and retention of females. Lipid residues in pots detect dairying directly, and the human genetics of lactase persistence tracks it independently.
ev: Age-at-death profiles; dairy lipid residues; lactase persistence genetics

l1: Sickles, hoes, digging sticks, ards — equipment for working soil and harvest.
l2: The tools set the ceiling on how much land one household can work, and that ceiling sets everything else: surplus, population, how many people can do something other than farm. Later, the shift from hand tools to animal traction raises the ceiling again by roughly an order of magnitude.
l3: Sickle blades develop a characteristic silica gloss from cutting cereal stems, identifiable under magnification. Ard marks survive as crossed scratch patterns preserved in buried soils beneath later monuments.
ev: Sickle gloss; preserved ard marks; tool assemblages

l1: Moving water to where the crops are.
l2: Irrigation makes dry land productive and decouples the harvest from rainfall. It is also the first technology that forces collective organisation: canals must be dug by many, maintained forever, and shared under rules. Some of the earliest written records anywhere are water allocation disputes.
l3: Canal systems survive as earthworks and are datable by their fills. Salinisation — the accumulation of salt that eventually ruins irrigated soil — is detectable in sediments and in a shift in crops from wheat to more salt-tolerant barley.
ev: Canal earthworks; sediment salinisation; crop-shift records
caution: Irrigation can degrade the land it feeds. Salinisation is documented in several early systems.

l1: Keeping a harvest dry, sealed and safe from rodents until next year.
l2: Grain stores well, which is exactly why it became the staple of state societies rather than more nutritious but perishable crops. A sealed granary holds a year of food, and a countable, taxable, seizable asset. It is hard to overstate how much of subsequent history follows from that property.
l3: Granaries appear as raised structures on post settings — the elevation keeps rodents out and air moving. Some at Pre-Pottery Neolithic sites in the Jordan Valley predate clear crop domestication, meaning storage came first.
ev: Raised granary structures; storage pits; sealed vessels

date: ≈ 11,000 years ago, independently in multiple regions
l1: Producing food deliberately instead of finding it.
l2: Agriculture raises calories per hectare enormously and lowers them per hour worked — farmers generally work harder than foragers for a less varied diet. What it buys is density and storability, and those two properties support everything that needs a lot of people in one place: cities, states, specialists, writing.
l3: Independent origins are documented in Southwest Asia, China, Mesoamerica, the Andes, New Guinea and elsewhere, each with different crops on different timelines. Charred plant assemblages, isotopes and ancient genomes converge on the same picture.
ev: Regional archaeobotanical sequences; isotopes; crop genomes
caution: Agriculture was not a single invention that spread from one place, and it was not obviously an improvement for the individuals who adopted it.

l1: More food than the people who grew it need to eat.
l2: Surplus is the hinge of this whole section. It is what pays for people who do not farm — priests, potters, soldiers, scribes, engineers — and therefore what makes specialisation, hierarchy and cities structurally possible. It is also the thing that can be taken, which is where states begin.
l3: Surplus is inferred from storage capacity relative to estimated population, and from the presence of full-time specialists who must have been fed by someone else. Later, written ration and tax records make it explicit.
ev: Storage-capacity estimates; specialist populations; ration records

l1: Treating ground as a divisible, ownable, improvable asset.
l2: Once land is improved — cleared, terraced, irrigated, manured — the improvement has to be defended, which turns territory into property. Fallow rotation, terracing and manuring are the techniques; boundaries, inheritance and land law are the institutions that grew around them.
l3: Field systems survive as boundary banks, walls and terraces, mappable from the air and from lidar. Manuring is detectable as scatters of domestic pottery spread across fields with the muck.
ev: Field boundaries; terraces; manuring scatters; lidar survey

l1: Enough households in one place that they must agree on rules.
l2: A village crosses a threshold that a camp does not: you now live permanently among people you did not choose and cannot avoid. Shared walls, shared water, shared waste and shared defence all need conventions, and the conventions need enforcement. Village life is where most social institutions were first worked out.
l3: Sites such as Çatalhöyük in Anatolia show dense agglomerated housing over many rebuild phases, with household-level storage and burial beneath floors — a settlement that is clearly permanent and clearly organised, but with no obvious central authority.
ev: Agglomerated house plans; rebuild sequences; household storage

l1: A village organised around a shared agricultural calendar.
l2: Farming synchronises people. Ploughing, sowing and harvest have narrow windows, and missing one costs a year — so labour must be pooled at exactly the same moments. That shared calendar becomes the backbone of communal ritual, obligation and, eventually, the formal year.
l3: Communal structures, shared threshing floors and standardised house layouts indicate coordination. Seasonal ritual sites aligned to solstices tie the agricultural calendar to the astronomical one.
ev: Communal facilities; standardised layouts; solstice alignments

l1: People who do one thing full-time and eat because others farm.
l2: Full-time specialists are where skill compounds. A potter who throws every day for thirty years reaches a level no part-timer reaches, and the same holds for metalworkers, scribes and builders. Every technically demanding object later in this graph implies somebody was fed to make it.
l3: Workshop areas with concentrated production debris, highly standardised products and specialist-only tools mark the transition. Burials with craft toolkits identify individuals by trade.
ev: Workshop debris; product standardisation; craft-tool burials

l1: Goods moving between people who each want what the other has.
l2: Trade lets a region use resources it does not have, and it moves ideas along with cargo — techniques, styles, scripts and diseases all travel the same routes. Long-distance exchange networks existed long before states, and they are among the best evidence that unrelated groups could sustain trust.
l3: Provenance science makes trade visible. Obsidian is geochemically fingerprinted to specific volcanic sources, so a blade found hundreds of kilometres away proves a route. Lead isotopes do the same for metals, amber and shell for other networks.
ev: Obsidian sourcing; lead-isotope provenance; exotic goods distribution
